notes.b: Inputs are what a family brings into the management process at the start: the demands made on it and the resources it has to meet them. Getting the inputs clear first matters because everything later depends on them.
points: Needs are necessities that must be met, such as food, shelter, warmth and clothing, so they come before everything else when resources are short.

Wants are things desired beyond necessities, such as a particular brand, a holiday or a new appliance. A want can be postponed or dropped when resources are short, which is the key difference from a need.
Goals are the outcomes the family sets out to achieve, such as a balanced weekly budget or a family meal on the table by six o'clock.
Values are what the family believes is important, and they shape which goals the family chooses.
Human resources are the time, energy, skills, knowledge and people in the family, who make and carry out decisions.

Material resources are equipment, ingredients, food, clothing, furniture and other household goods used in the task. Marking schemes also list economic resources (money: income and savings) and environmental resources (space, surroundings and community facilities).
Inputs are the starting point, so clear goals are the first step: a poorly defined or vague need or goal at this stage leads to a result that does not meet the family's needs.
notes.tip: Keep needs and wants apart: a need must be met, a want can be postponed. Resources, like needs, wants, goals and values, belong under inputs, not outputs.

notes.b: Throughputs are the actions a family takes to change its inputs into outputs. There are three: planning, organising and implementing.
points: Planning means gathering information, considering the alternatives, weighing them up and deciding on a course of action.
Organising means allocating tasks and responsibilities (who does what and when), arranging the resources each task needs and communicating with those involved.
Implementing means putting the plan into action, such as booking, buying, cooking or cleaning.
Changes are made during implementing as needs arise, such as an unexpected guest or a shortage of an ingredient, because no plan covers everything.
A plan lists the steps in order and the resources each step needs, so that work can be checked against it.
Decision-making and communication run through all three throughputs, because choices have to be made and shared at every stage.
notes.tip: Throughputs are actions, not results. Students often put evaluation under throughputs, but it is an output.

notes.b: Outputs are the results produced by the throughputs, and they are judged against the inputs, especially the goals set at the start. Outputs also feed back into the next cycle, so the framework is a loop and not a straight line.
points: Goals achieved: whether the goals were met and whether needs were fulfilled and wants satisfied.
Changes in values, goals and standards: the experience may change what the family thinks is important or reasonable, or show that a goal or standard was unrealistic and needs to be revised.
Satisfaction: whether family members are happy with the result and whether their needs and wants were met.

Evaluation: an assessment of whether resources were used effectively, whether the task was organised efficiently, and whether time, money and energy were used well and the result met the family's needs.
Effective use of feedback: what is learned is fed back into the system as an input to the next cycle, so that the next round of planning is improved.
notes.tip: Do not draw the framework as a line that ends at outputs: say that feedback returns to the inputs. Outputs for the exam are goals reached, values changed, needs met, wants fulfilled, resources used effectively and people satisfied.

notes.h: Applying the management framework to a named event (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The framework can be used to plan any event or task, such as a graduation, a holiday, a party, a meal or a house move. It suits meal planning, money and home management, problem solving and decision-making. A family birthday party is used here as the example.
points: Inputs: the need is a celebration; the goal is a happy party for a child; the want is a particular cake; the human resources are time and help from relatives; the material resources are food, decorations and invitations; the money available sets the budget.
Throughputs: planning the guest list and the budget; organising who buys food, who prepares the room and who sends invitations; implementing the plan and adjusting for extra guests.
Outputs: whether the goal of a happy party was achieved, whether the money was kept within budget, whether members were satisfied, and what would improve the next event.
Feedback from the outputs is recorded so that the next party is planned more efficiently, which is why the framework is a cycle.
notes.tip: In an applied question, write a fully worked example with at least two event-specific points for each of inputs, throughputs and outputs, because marks are given per point in each of the three parts.

notes.b: A decision is a choice of one course of action from a set of alternatives. Families make decisions all the time, so a clear method and the involvement of everyone affected make the management process work better.
points: The sequence of decision-making is: identify the problem or need, gather information, list the options, weigh each option against the goals and resources, choose one and act on it, then review the result.
Review after acting: check whether the decision achieved the goal, and record what should be done differently next time, so that evaluation gives lessons for the future.
Sharing information and ideas before a decision allows the family to allocate tasks fairly and to share values, views and concerns.
Decisions made with the views of all members help to resolve conflict and issues and build commitment to the outcome.
Decision-making helps the family achieve its goals and improves the efficiency of its work.
Discussion gives members a broader view of the issues, because each person sees the problem differently.
Decisions are easier when the family's values and goals have been agreed beforehand, because options can then be judged against them.
notes.tip: When asked to explain the importance of decision-making, give separate developed points such as sharing information and ideas, allocating tasks, resolving conflict, achieving goals, improving efficiency and a broader view.

notes.b: Communication is the sharing of information, ideas, values and concerns between family members. Without it, decisions made by one person never reach the people who have to carry them out.
points: Communication is needed at every stage: agreeing goals in the inputs, allocating tasks in organising, reporting progress in implementing and giving feedback.
Open discussion of what is and is not working provides the feedback that is used to evaluate the outputs.
Practical methods include a family discussion or meeting, notes, a shared written list, a shared calendar and messaging.

Poor communication leads to duplicated or missed tasks, misunderstandings and conflict, because members do not know what has been decided or who is responsible. A decision that is not communicated to every member can lead to duplicated work, missed tasks and conflict.

notes.h: Planning routines for modern patterns of living
notes.b: Families today live in many different ways, so a routine has to be planned around how the household actually works. Sharing the work fairly is what makes a routine last.
points: Modern patterns of living include two working adults, shift workers, lone-parent households, a parent working from home, and children in childcare or after-school activities, and routines must be fitted around these.
Work sharing: tasks such as cooking, shopping, laundry and cleaning are divided between members, so no one person carries the whole load.
Responsibility for family tasks: each member is given a defined task for which they are accountable, matched to age and ability.
Delegation: an adult passes a task to another member and gives them the instructions, time and resources needed to complete it, and trusts them to do it.
Gender equity: household tasks are shared on the basis of ability, availability and fairness rather than assigned by sex.
Checklists for routines: a daily or weekly checklist lists each task, who completes it and when it is due, so that nothing is forgotten.
Work schedules: a written timetable, such as a weekly cleaning rota or a meal planner, shows the sequence of tasks and who is responsible for each one.
notes.tip: To describe how a family could share work, include work sharing, delegation, a rota or checklist and gender equity.

notes.b: Money is only one resource. Several others help a family run a good management system, and each makes its own contribution.
points: Time: allows planning and avoids waste; tasks are completed more efficiently when time is scheduled.
People: family members make and carry out decisions and tasks.
Skills and knowledge: support problem solving, healthy meals and budgeting.
Equipment: saves time and energy; a washing machine, for example, replaces hours of hand washing.
Human energy: allows tasks to be completed in an acceptable and harmonious way.
notes.tip: When asked for resources other than money, name each one and say how it helps the management system: people, time, skills and knowledge, equipment, human energy.

keyTerms.definition: The model of a management system made up of inputs, throughputs and outputs.
The resources, needs, wants and goals a family brings into the management process.
The planning, organising and implementing actions that change inputs into outputs.
The results of the management process, including goals achieved, satisfaction and evaluation.
Necessities that must be met, such as food, shelter and warmth.
The outcomes a family sets out to achieve.
Passing a task to another member together with the instructions and resources needed to complete it.
Information about the result of an action, used to improve the next cycle of management.
Choosing one course of action from a set of alternatives after weighing them against goals and resources.
The sharing of information, ideas, values and concerns between family members.

questions.prompt: Name the three stages of the management process and describe how one of them could be used when planning a family meal.
questions.model: Stages (3 marks): inputs (needs, wants, goals, human and material resources); throughputs (planning, organising, implementing); outputs (goals achieved, satisfaction, evaluation and feedback). Description (3 marks), for example: planning the weekly menu within the food budget, using the family's needs and time; organising who shops and who cooks; implementing by preparing the meal and adjusting for a late arrival; evaluating whether the meal met the family's needs and whether the money was used well.

questions.prompt: Using the management framework, explain how a family could plan and evaluate a family holiday. Refer to decision-making and communication in your answer.
questions.model: Inputs: the need for a break, goals such as rest and family time, wants such as a particular destination, human resources (time, skills, energy of members) and material resources and money that set the budget. Throughputs: planning involves gathering information on costs and options and deciding on a course of action; organising allocates tasks such as booking, packing and arranging transport; implementing carries out the plan and adjusts for changes. Decision-making: identify the options, weigh them against the budget and goals, choose one and review it. Communication: members share information and views so that decisions are agreed and tasks are not duplicated or missed. Outputs: evaluate whether the goals were achieved, whether the budget was kept, whether all members were satisfied and record feedback for planning the next holiday.
